Erased but Exploitable: Black-box Embedding-Aware Prompting Against Unlearned Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

1st Arian Komaei Koma Affiliation: Department of Computer Engineering

ariankomaei@gmail.com    2nd Seyed Amir Kasaei Affiliation: Department of Computer Engineering

Abstract

Machine unlearning aims to remove specific concepts from pretrained text-to-image diffusion models, yet several white- and black-box attacks have been introduced to make the model generate such unlearned concepts. These attacks, nevertheless, do not assume a realistic threat model, i.e. they either assume access to the model weights, or result in gibberish adversarial prompts that could be easily detected even through naive rule-based safeguarding. We aim to address this gap in this paper. We introduce BEAP—a black-box, embedding-aware adversarial prompting attack that leverages a large language model (LLM) to iteratively generate effective adversarial prompts and exploit such hidden vulnerabilities. BEAP performs an embedding-aware search in text space, combining multiple reward signals—unlearned concept presence, text–image alignment, and image quality—to refine generated prompts. Unlike previous attack methods, BEAP keeps its prompts undetectable to safety filters while producing high-quality images. Across five unlearning methods, BEAP achieves a macro-averaged ASR of 97.8% under the held-out OpenNSFW2 evaluation, exceeding the white-box UDA baseline by 41.6 percentage points (56.2% to 97.8%). Counting unsuccessful searches at the full 100-query budget, BEAP uses 32.1 image-generation queries per evaluated prompt on average under this criterion. Warning: This paper contains model outputs that may be offensive or upsetting in nature.

Index Terms: 
machine unlearning, text-to-image diffusion models, adversarial prompting, black-box attacks, generative AI safety.

I Introduction

Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have rapidly advanced, enabling realistic image synthesis directly from text inputs. Models such as DALL·E 3 [1], Stable Diffusion [2, 3, 4], and MidJourney [5] show strong semantic understanding and flexible visual generation across diverse domains. However, because these systems are trained on large-scale web data, they can also be misused to generate inappropriate or unsafe content, raising significant ethical concerns [6, 7, 8]. To mitigate these risks, recent diffusion systems incorporate Not Safe For Work (NSFW) safeguards before or after generation to filter problematic prompts or outputs [9, 10, 11, 12, 13].

External filters, however, are model-agnostic, post-hoc interventions rather than direct remedies for unsafe model behavior. Prior studies have shown that these safeguards may fail to prevent diffusion models from producing harmful outputs [14, 15, 16]. They can also be circumvented through jailbreaking attacks [17, 18, 19, 20]. In a T2I jailbreak attack, an adversary transforms a disallowed NSFW prompt into a less conspicuous prompt that bypasses the safeguard while eliciting similar unsafe content. These findings demonstrate that external safety mechanisms alone cannot reliably prevent unsafe generation.

To address this limitation, another line of work has explored machine unlearning [21]: the selective removal of specific knowledge or concepts from a trained model without retraining it from scratch. Unlike safeguards that filter a model’s inputs or outputs, unlearning seeks to modify the model itself so that it no longer generates the unwanted concept while preserving its overall generative ability. Methods such as ESD [14], SPM [22], MACE [23], CA [24], SalUn [25], and SLD [7] fine-tune or otherwise modify model parameters to suppress a concept or redirect it toward a neutral alternative. Although these approaches can reduce explicit visual traces of unwanted content, they do not always guarantee complete forgetting; residual representations may remain encoded in the model [26, 27, 28]. As illustrated in Section A, unlearned models can regenerate a target concept in response to paraphrased prompts, suggesting that the concept has been suppressed rather than fully removed.

Follow-up studies, including QF-Attack [28], Generate-or-Not [29], and Ring-a-Bell [27], show that these residual representations can be exploited. UnlearnDiffAtk (UDA), introduced by Generate-or-Not, is a white-box attack that requires access to the victim model during prompt optimization, limiting its applicability when only model queries are available. Ring-a-Bell [27] and QF-Attack instead search in an embedding space, but they require information about the target model’s text encoder, which may be unavailable in realistic deployments.

Moreover, existing attacks often generate semantically meaningless or low-quality prompts with abnormally high perplexity, meaning that a standard language model assigns the text very low probability. Such prompts can be detected by lightweight safeguards based on perplexity or gibberish detection [30].

Consequently, existing attacks face important practical limitations: they require privileged model access, depend on prior knowledge of the target architecture, or produce conspicuously unnatural prompts.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce BEAP, a black-box attack framework that uses a large language model (LLM) to search directly in natural-language space. This approach allows BEAP to explore diverse, semantically meaningful paraphrases without explicitly optimizing prompt embeddings in ways that can produce unnatural or nonsensical text.

BEAP iteratively queries the unlearned model and uses an LLM to refine candidate prompts based on feedback about concept presence, text–image alignment, and image quality. To focus the search, we also provide the LLM with a set of surrogate terms whose embeddings are close to the target concept in an external text-embedding space. By combining natural-language generation, reward-guided refinement, and embedding-aware lexical guidance, BEAP exposes residual concept representations without requiring access to the victim model’s weights or gradients. Its prompts also remain substantially more natural under the evaluated perplexity and gibberish-detection metrics than those produced by prior attacks.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose an LLM-driven, query-only black-box attack on unlearned text-to-image diffusion models that generates human-readable adversarial prompts.

  • •

    We design a reward-guided iterative search that combines multiple feedback signals to refine candidate prompts.

  • •

    We introduce an embedding-aware lexical guidance component that uses semantic proximity to the target concept to improve text-space exploration.

  • •

    We demonstrate that five representative unlearning methods retain exploitable concept information: BEAP recovers the target concept with natural-language prompts while satisfying the evaluated concept-presence, alignment, and image-quality criteria.

II Related Works

II-A Unlearning Methods

Machine unlearning (MU) [31][32][21] aims to remove specific concepts, styles, or data influences from a trained text-to-image (T2I) diffusion model without retraining it from scratch. Early methods such as ESD [14] and CA [24] focused on modifying UNet architecture though finetuning negative guidance. UCE [33] introduced a training-free unified approach using closed-form solutions for simultaneous debiasing, style erasure, and content moderation. SPM [22] proposed an adapter-based approach using “concept-SemiPermeable Membranes” that can be flexibly transferred across different models without re-tuning. Other approaches include EDiff [34], which formulates unlearning as a constrained optimization problem to preserve model utility. MACE [23] proposes tuning the prompt-related projection matrices of the cross-attention blocks in the UNet architecture using LoRA modules. Reliable concept erasing via Lightweight Erasers (Receler) [35] introduces a new component into the neural network, the eraser, that acts on the cross-attention layers of the U-Net, and that is trained as in ESD [14].

II-B Adversarial Prompting Against T2I models

One line of work targets the original pretrained T2I diffusion models via jailbreaking, e.g., JailFuzzer [19] and SneakyPrompt [18], which rely on iterative prompt refinement through repeated queries to the target model. A complementary line of research investigates attacks on models that have undergone unlearning. Several studies have shown that current unlearning procedures remain vulnerable to carefully crafted prompts [28, 26, 27, 29]. In the white-box setting, Generate-or-Not proposes UnlearnDiffAtk (UDA) [29], which uses privileged access to the victim model to optimize adversarial prompts that recover erased concepts. P4D [36] similarly uses white-box optimization to identify problematic prompts. The most closely related approaches to ours—Ring-A-Bell [27] and MMA [37]—operate in a black-box setting with access to the victim model’s text encoder, searching in the embedding space for adversarial prompts that reactivate seemingly unlearned content.

III BEAP: Black-Box Embedding-Aware Adversarial Prompting

Figure 1 presents BEAP, our framework for generating adversarial prompts against unlearned text-to-image diffusion models. BEAP conducts a black-box search for concepts that were not fully removed during unlearning. Rather than optimizing arbitrary tokens that may produce garbled text, it uses an LLM to generate natural, human-readable prompts. The LLM receives feedback about concept presence, text–image alignment, and image quality. An additional embedding-guided component steers the LLM toward words that are semantically related to the target concept. Together, these components produce interpretable adversarial prompts without requiring access to the victim model’s weights, gradients, or other internal information.

III-A Threat Model

We consider an attacker with query-only access to a deployed, unlearned text-to-image diffusion model. The attacker knows which concept the model is intended to have removed and possesses an initial prompt that describes this concept. The attacker may submit arbitrary natural-language prompts but observes only the images returned by the victim model. We assume no access to model weights, gradients, activations, attention maps, training or unlearning data, the unlearning algorithm, the victim model’s text encoder, or internal safety and confidence scores.

The attacker may use independently available tools, including an LLM for prompt refinement, concept detectors for scoring generated images, and an off-the-shelf text encoder for constructing the adversarial similarity vocabulary. These components are neither extracted from nor accessed through the victim model. In particular, the embedding-guidance component uses a separately obtained pretrained encoder and does not require the parameters of the victim model’s text encoder. Accordingly, black-box describes the attacker’s interaction with the victim diffusion model: BEAP relies only on prompt queries and returned images rather than privileged access to the victim’s internals.

We impose a fixed query budget rather than assuming unrestricted access. With Q=10Q=10 candidate prompts per iteration and at most ℐ=10\mathcal{I}=10 iterations, BEAP makes no more than Q​ℐ=100Q\mathcal{I}=100 image-generation queries for each initial prompt. The search terminates early when its stopping criteria are satisfied. Our experiments do not model provider-specific rate limits or adaptive throttling; each method is evaluated under its stated total query budget. The threat model therefore assumes that repeated queries are permitted within this budget. Deployments that allow substantially fewer queries, delay feedback, or do not return generated images are outside the scope of this evaluation.

III-B LLM-Driven Semantic Adversarial Search

III-B1 LLM-Guided Iterative Search

At the first iteration (t=1t{=}1), the LLM ℒ\mathcal{L} receives an instruction describing the target concept together with the initial prompt p(0)p^{(0)}. It generates QQ diverse paraphrases, denoted by {pi(t)}i=1Q\{p_{i}^{(t)}\}_{i=1}^{Q}.

Each candidate prompt pi(t)p_{i}^{(t)} is submitted to the unlearned diffusion model ℳu\mathcal{M}_{u}, which produces the corresponding image ℳu​(pi(t))\mathcal{M}_{u}(p_{i}^{(t)}). We evaluate each prompt–image pair using the three reward signals described in Section III-B2.

After scoring all candidates, we sample SS prompts according to their ImageReward scores [38], assigning higher selection probabilities to candidates with higher scores. We use ImageReward for this sampling step because it provides a comparatively stable measure of text–image correspondence during iterative optimization [39].

Specifically, we use softmax sampling with temperature TT to balance exploitation of high-scoring candidates with exploration of the text space:

Softmax​(pi(t),T)=exp⁡(R⁡(p(0),ℳu​(pi(t)))/T)∑j=1Qexp⁡(R⁡(p(0),ℳu​(pj(t)))/T),\text{Softmax}(p_{i}^{(t)},T)=\frac{\exp\left(R(p^{(0)},\mathcal{M}_{u}(p_{i}^{(t)}))/T\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{Q}\exp\left(R(p^{(0)},\mathcal{M}_{u}(p_{j}^{(t)}))/T\right)}, (1)

Here, RR denotes the ImageReward score between the generated image ℳu​(pi(t))\mathcal{M}_{u}(p_{i}^{(t)}) and the initial prompt p(0)p^{(0)}. We provide the selected prompts and their feedback from all three reward models to ℒ\mathcal{L} as structured input for the next refinement step. The LLM then produces a new batch of QQ refined paraphrases, {pi(t+1)}i=1Q\{p_{i}^{(t+1)}\}_{i=1}^{Q}, as illustrated in Figure 2.

During optimization, ℒ\mathcal{L} does not receive a single summed reward. Instead, it receives separate feedback signals for target-concept presence, text–image alignment, and image quality, allowing it to consider their interplay when refining the next batch of prompts.

As shown in Figure 1(B), the process continues until at least one prompt satisfies all three reward thresholds or the maximum number of iterations ℐ\mathcal{I} is reached. If multiple candidates satisfy all thresholds in the terminating iteration, we return the candidate with the highest sum of the three scores. If no candidate satisfies all thresholds, we select the best-performing prompt lexicographically, prioritizing concept presence, followed by text–image alignment and image quality.

III-B2 Reward Signals for Prompt Refinement

For each generated image, we compute three complementary scores that capture distinct aspects of text-to-image generation: (i) a Concept Detection Score, obtained from a concept detector such as NudeNet [40] or DINOv2 [41], which measures the presence of the target concept or object; (ii) ImageReward [38], which measures semantic alignment between the generated image and the initial prompt; and (iii) an Aesthetic Score [42], which measures the perceptual quality of the generated image.

A prompt is considered successful only when all three scores exceed their corresponding thresholds: τdet\tau_{\text{det}}, τimg\tau_{\text{img}}, and τaes\tau_{\text{aes}}. By jointly enforcing concept presence, semantic alignment, and image quality, this multi-signal criterion reduces reliance on any single potentially biased objective and helps limit reward hacking [43, 44].

III-C Adversarial Similarity-Based Search

Although the LLM can refine prompts through natural-language paraphrasing, it has no direct information about how individual words relate to the target concept in an embedding space. We therefore construct an adversarial similarity vocabulary: a set of words that an external text encoder f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) places near the target concept.

This vocabulary steers ℒ\mathcal{L} toward the semantic neighborhood of the target concept and focuses the search on regions in which unlearning may be incomplete.

We first define the following set of paired prompts:

𝒟c={(𝐏1c,𝐏1c),…,(𝐏Nc,𝐏Nc)}\mathcal{D}_{c}=\{(\mathbf{P}_{1}^{c},\mathbf{P}_{1}^{\cancel{c}}),\ldots,(\mathbf{P}_{N}^{c},\mathbf{P}_{N}^{\cancel{c}})\}

Each pair contains a prompt 𝐏ic\mathbf{P}_{i}^{c} that expresses the target concept and a neutralized counterpart 𝐏ic\mathbf{P}_{i}^{\cancel{c}} in which the primary concept term is removed or replaced with neutral language (e.g., “naked person” versus “a person”). We compute the difference between the embeddings in each pair and average these differences to obtain the adversarial sentence-level concept vector:

cadv=1N​∑i=1N(f⁡(𝐏ic)−f⁡(𝐏ic)),c_{\text{adv}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big(f(\mathbf{P}_{i}^{c})-f(\mathbf{P}_{i}^{\cancel{c}})\big),

where f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) maps a sentence to its embedding representation.

Paired sentences capture the target concept across multiple contexts rather than representing it with a single keyword. Consequently, cadvc_{\text{adv}} describes broader semantic content associated with the target concept and provides a more robust signal for similarity-based retrieval. As illustrated in Figure 3, the retrieved top-kk words steer the LLM toward nearby semantic regions that may still elicit the target concept.

We then compute the cosine similarity between cadvc_{\text{adv}} and each word embedding f⁡(vj)f(v_{j}) in a reference vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V} (e.g., the Oxford 3000):

Cos​(cadv,vj)=cadv⋅f⁡(vj)‖cadv‖​‖f⁡(vj)‖,vj∈𝒱.\text{Cos}(c_{\text{adv}},v_{j})=\frac{c_{\text{adv}}\cdot f(v_{j})}{\|c_{\text{adv}}\|\,\|f(v_{j})\|},\quad v_{j}\in\mathcal{V}.

The kk words with the highest similarity scores form the adversarial similarity vocabulary. We provide this vocabulary to ℒ\mathcal{L} as additional lexical guidance (Figure 1 (A)).

IV Experiments & Results

IV-A Experimental setup

We evaluate on the 200 highest-nudity prompts from the I2P benchmark[7], using the original seeds and guidance scales to ensure reproducibility. All methods are applied to Stable Diffusion v1.4  [2] with safety filters disabled to expose the inherent vulnerability of the unlearned models. Consistent with the threat model in Section III-A, BEAP accesses each target model only by submitting prompts and observing its generated images. We compare our method, BEAP, and its variant without embedding guidance (BEAP (w/o EG)), against standard unlearning baselines: UCE[33], ESD[14], MACE[23], SPM[22], and Receler[35].

For the black-box attack baseline, we adopt Ring-a-Bell [27] with its default evolutionary configuration and set the prompt length to 16. We additionally evaluate UnlearnDiffAtk (UDA), introduced by Generate-or-Not [29], as a white-box baseline. UDA requires privileged access to the victim model during prompt optimization and therefore falls outside our query-only threat model; we include it to compare BEAP against an attack with stronger access assumptions. BEAP uses DeepSeek-V3.1 [45] as the default LLM to generate and refine candidate prompts over ℐ=10\mathcal{I}=10 iterations with Q=10Q=10 candidates per step, selecting the top S=3S=3 via ImageReward-based softmax sampling. During search, candidate prompts are scored using ImageReward, Aesthetic Score, and a concept detector: NudeNet for nudity and DINOv2 for object unlearning. For DINOv2, an image is considered to contain the target object when “golf ball” is its top-1 predicted class. To avoid evaluating concept recovery with the same detector used for optimization, we independently rescore nudity generations with OpenNSFW2 [46] and object generations with a pretrained ResNet-50 classifier [47]. OpenNSFW2 marks an image as containing nudity when its NSFW score exceeds 0.5, while ResNet-50 marks object recovery when “golf ball” is the top-1 predicted class. All reported results are averaged over three independent runs.

We report two Attack Success Rates (ASRs). ASROpenNSFW2{}_{\text{OpenNSFW2}} measures nudity presence using the held-out OpenNSFW2 classifier, while ASRResNet-50{}_{\text{ResNet-50}} measures object presence using the held-out ResNet-50 classifier in the exploratory object-unlearning experiment. ASRAll{}_{\text{All}} additionally requires the ImageReward and Aesthetic Score thresholds to be met. Because ImageReward and Aesthetic Score also guide the search, we treat their reported values as optimization-objective diagnostics rather than fully independent evaluations of alignment and image quality. Finally, we evaluate prompt detectability using perplexity and a gibberish detector [30]. The average-iteration columns report the stopping iteration among successful searches; we separately report a query average that includes unsuccessful searches at the full budget. Additional setup details appear in Section B.

IV-B Experiments on Concept Removal Models

The results in Table I highlight several key observations. First, unlearning alone is insufficient: all “w/o attack” models exhibit non-zero ASROpenNSFW2{}_{\text{OpenNSFW2}}, showing that residual traces of the concept persist even without adversarial prompting. Ring-a-Bell can occasionally re-activate the concept under ASROpenNSFW2{}_{\text{OpenNSFW2}}, but it consistently fails under the stricter ASRAll{}_{\text{All}} evaluation. Its outputs typically violate either alignment or aesthetic thresholds, resulting in an ASRAll{}_{\text{All}} of zero for every unlearning method. The white-box UDA baseline improves over Ring-a-Bell, reaching ASROpenNSFW2{}_{\text{OpenNSFW2}} values of 22–70% and ASRAll{}_{\text{All}} values of 10–32%. Nevertheless, despite its stronger access assumptions, UDA remains substantially less effective than both BEAP (w/o EG) and BEAP. They achieve high ASROpenNSFW2{}_{\text{OpenNSFW2}} (generally 86–99%) and maintain strong ASRAll{}_{\text{All}}, indicating that the recovered images satisfy both the held-out nudity detector and the search objectives for alignment and visual quality.

While vulnerability varies across unlearning techniques—SPM and ESD being easier to break and MACE or Receler showing stronger resistance—none of the evaluated methods demonstrate robustness against BEAP. Although UCE reports a much lower ASRAll{}_{\text{All}}, this primarily reflects the model’s poor image quality: UCE’s own outputs score noticeably low on both Aesthetic and ImageReward metrics (Table II), which explains the large gap between its ASROpenNSFW2{}_{\text{OpenNSFW2}} and ASRAll{}_{\text{All}}. Even when the concept reappears, the generated image often fails the quality or alignment thresholds required in our evaluation.

Across all settings, ASRAll{}_{\text{All}} remains lower than ASROpenNSFW2{}_{\text{OpenNSFW2}}. This gap reflects cases where the concept is present but the generated output fails the ImageReward or Aesthetic thresholds, particularly for unlearned models that tend to produce noisy or poorly aligned images.

Finally, embedding guidance provides a consistent advantage: BEAP typically improves success rates or reduces the number of iterations compared to BEAP (w/o EG). Overall, these findings show that diffusion models remain highly vulnerable to natural-language adversarial prompting even after concept removal procedures.

Macro-averaged across the five unlearning methods, BEAP attains 97.8% ASROpenNSFW2{}_{\text{OpenNSFW2}}, compared with 56.2% for the white-box UDA baseline, an absolute improvement of 41.6 percentage points. Since each iteration evaluates Q=10Q=10 candidates, we also convert stopping iterations into victim-model image-generation queries. Counting every unsuccessful search as exhausting the full ℐ=10\mathcal{I}=10 iterations, BEAP uses approximately 32.1 queries per evaluated prompt on average under the OpenNSFW2 success criterion. This macro-average is computed from the rounded per-model ASR and successful-search iteration averages in Table I; it therefore includes both successful and unsuccessful attack attempts.

IV-C Image Quality and Alignment

We summarize the visual fidelity and text–image consistency of generated outputs using the Aesthetic and ImageReward scores, reported over both all generated prompts and the subset of successful generations that satisfy all thresholds. Since both metrics are used during prompt optimization, this analysis measures satisfaction of BEAP’s search objectives and should not be interpreted as a held-out evaluation. The results in Table II show consistent trends across all unlearned diffusion models.

Ring-a-Bell produces noticeably degraded outputs: both its Aesthetic and ImageReward values fall below those of the unlearned backbones, and it scores zero in all “Success” columns, indicating that even when it partially reactivates the concept, the resulting images are too low-quality or poorly aligned to satisfy our criteria. By contrast, BEAP recovers the concept while preserving visual quality. In addition, for every unlearning method, BEAP achieves higher Aesthetic and ImageReward scores than Ring-a-Bell and frequently exceeds the backbone’s own “w/o attack” values.

UDA generally improves visual quality over Ring-a-Bell, but its ImageReward scores across all generations remain lower than those of both BEAP variants. Its successful outputs exceed the required quality and alignment thresholds, yet their scores remain close to those thresholds, helping explain the gap between UDA and BEAP under ASRAll{}_{\text{All}}.

Overall, although unlearning procedures tend to reduce image fidelity, BEAP (w/o EG) and BEAP reliably restore both alignment and image quality while reintroducing the target concept, producing coherent, natural, and visually well-formed generations.

IV-D Detectability of Adversarial Prompts

We assess how detectable the generated prompts are by measuring their linguistic naturalness using two indicators: Gibberish Detection Rate (GDR) (lower is better) and Mean Perplexity (lower indicates more natural text). As shown in Table III, Ring-a-Bell produces highly incoherent prompts, reflected in its maximum GDR of 100% and extremely large perplexity (4736). Such values place its prompts far outside the range of normal language, making them trivial for simple perplexity- or gibberish-based filters to detect.

In contrast, BEAP and BEAP (w/o EG) generate prompts that remain within the distribution of natural human-written text. Their perplexity values (569–653) stay close to the I2P reference prompts (505), and their GDR (26% for BEAP and 33% for BEAP (w/o EG)) are even lower than the original I2P prompts. This indicates that the generated text is fully readable and grammatically well-formed. Among the two variants, BEAP produces the most natural prompts on average, benefiting from its embedding-guided refinement.

Overall, these results show that BEAP produces linguistically natural adversarial prompts. Unlike prior attacks that rely on incoherent or out-of-distribution text, these prompts are difficult for lightweight text-based safety mechanisms to detect.

IV-E Object Unlearning as an Exploratory Case

We further evaluate BEAP on an object-level unlearning task by targeting the “golf ball” category. Experiments are conducted on unlearned versions of UCE and Receler, with comparisons to their original models and to Ring-a-Bell. During optimization, DINOv2 provides the object-presence feedback supplied to BEAP. For held-out evaluation, we instead use a pretrained ResNet-50 classifier [47], preventing the optimization detector from also determining the reported object ASR. We crafted 50 evaluation prompts using GPT-5.1 [48] that contain the phrase “golf ball”. The results in Table IV reveal several important observations.

First, UCE exhibits high ASR even without any attack, achieving 88% under ResNet-50 and 54% under the stricter “All” criterion. This indicates that the unlearning process for this object category was largely unsuccessful: the model continues to regenerate golf balls under the original evaluation prompts. In contrast, Receler shows complete suppression under its “w/o attack” setting, with ASR of 0 across both metrics.

Ring-a-Bell provides only weak reactivation of the object and performs especially poorly on Receler. By comparison, BEAP (w/o EG) and BEAP reliably recover the object on both backbones, achieving high ASR values while requiring only a small number of iterations. The embedding-guided variant BEAP provides a modest improvement over its ablation.

Overall, this exploratory case demonstrates that current unlearning techniques struggle not only with safety-sensitive concepts but also with ordinary object categories, and that BEAP remains effective across both scenarios.

IV-F Qualitative Results

To visualize the effect of our attack, Figure 4 shows qualitative examples across all five unlearning backbones evaluated in our study: UCE, ESD, MACE, SPM, and Receler. For each model, we include the output generated from the original I2P prompt, from Ring-a-Bell, and from our full method BEAP. The comparison highlights both the visual quality of generated images and the meaningfulness of their corresponding prompts.

Across all backbones, Ring-a-Bell produces garbled, incoherent prompts that result in distorted or low-quality images with poor semantic alignment. Although these prompts may occasionally trigger the removed concept, the generated images generally lack structure, realism, or consistency with the intended description.

In contrast, BEAP consistently generates fluent, human-readable prompts that preserve clear semantic intent. The resulting images are visually coherent, aesthetically high-quality, and well aligned with the adversarial prompt. This holds uniformly across UCE, ESD, MACE, SPM, and Receler, demonstrating that BEAP restores both alignment and fidelity even in models that underwent different concept-removal procedures.

These qualitative observations reinforce our quantitative findings: despite unlearning, all five diffusion backbones retain residual representations of the removed concept, and BEAP can reliably surface them using natural-language prompts without sacrificing image quality.

V Conclusion

This work examined the reliability of current unlearning techniques for text-to-image diffusion models and found that they remain highly vulnerable. Despite attempts to remove target concepts, unlearned models can still regenerate them under simple phrasing changes, indicating only partial concept erasure. We introduced BEAP, a black-box adversarial prompting framework that combines LLM-based refinement, multi-signal rewards, and embedding-guided lexical exploration. BEAP generates natural prompts, high-quality images, and consistently achieves strong attack success across all major unlearning methods. Our analysis further extends to object-level unlearning, where similar weaknesses persist. Overall, these findings demonstrate that current unlearning pipelines are significantly more vulnerable than expected, highlighting the need for more reliable and verifiable approaches to concept removal in diffusion models.

VI Open Science

An anonymized artifact repository will accompany this submission. It will contain the implementation of BEAP, prompt-generation and evaluation scripts, experiment configurations, random seeds, and instructions for reproducing the reported quantitative results. We will also provide sanitized representative prompts and aggregate evaluation outputs. Because the study concerns the generation of safety-sensitive imagery, explicit generated content and any material that would unnecessarily facilitate misuse will be shared only to the extent required for scientific verification and under appropriate access controls. The released materials will document these exclusions and their rationale.

VII LLM Usage Considerations

Large language models are an integral component of the proposed method rather than a substitute for scientific evaluation. BEAP uses DeepSeek-V3.1 to generate and iteratively refine candidate adversarial prompts from structured instructions and numerical reward feedback. The object-unlearning exploratory study additionally used GPT-5.1 to construct an initial set of prompts containing the target object. All generated prompts were subsequently evaluated with the fixed experimental pipeline described in this paper; experimental measurements, tables, and conclusions were not accepted solely on the basis of LLM output.

LLM behavior can vary across model versions, providers, and decoding settings. To support reproducibility, the artifact will include the complete prompt templates, model identifiers, decoding parameters, query budgets, and retained outputs used in the experiments. Our experiments use pretrained hosted models only for inference and impose a fixed budget of ten candidates over at most ten iterations, avoiding additional LLM training and limiting unnecessary computation.

OpenAI Codex was used during manuscript preparation to assist with language, organization, and LaTeX editing. The authors reviewed and revised the resulting text and take full responsibility for the paper’s content, claims, and citations.

VIII Ethical Considerations

This research focuses on exposing security vulnerabilities in text-to-image diffusion models with the explicit goal of strengthening these systems rather than enabling misuse. To reduce the risk of harmful applications, certain implementation details of our attack have been deliberately omitted or presented at a high level.

We strongly encourage model developers and researchers to use these findings responsibly to improve the robustness of unlearning techniques and the safety of generative models. Ethical awareness is essential when working with powerful AI systems, particularly those capable of producing realistic imagery. We advocate for a balance between scientific innovation and ethical responsibility, including transparent reporting practices that emphasize societal impact and misuse prevention.

Appendix A Vulnerability Analysis

We assess the vulnerability of two concept-removal methods, UCE and Receler, to simple prompt paraphrasing. For each model, we use a prompt describing the unlearned concept and then provide a paraphrased version of the same description.

As shown in Figure 5, even small changes in wording are enough to bring back the supposedly unlearned concept. Although these models were trained to remove the concept of nudity, they still respond correctly to a paraphrased prompt expressing the same meaning. This indicates that current unlearning techniques do not eliminate the underlying concept from the model; instead, they weaken specific expressions of it. Once the phrasing shifts, the model can still access and regenerate the concept.

Appendix B Additional Experimental setup

Dataset.

Experiments are conducted using prompts selected from the I2P benchmark [7]. Specifically, we choose the 200 prompts with the highest nudity percentage to ensure a strong association with the target unlearned concept. For each prompt, we use the corresponding seed and guidance scale provided in the dataset to generate images, ensuring consistent initialization and reproducibility across all evaluated methods.

Unlearned Models.

We compare BEAP and its variant without embedding guidance, BEAP (w/o EG), against UCE [33], ESD [14], MACE [23], SPM [22], and Receler [35]. All referenced unlearning methods were originally implemented on Stable Diffusion v1.4 [2], so we use the same backbone for a consistent comparison. Following Section I, we evaluate the inherent vulnerability of unlearned models rather than Stable Diffusion’s initial safeguards. We therefore disable all safety mechanisms.

Baseline Attack Models.

For our black-box attack baseline, we select Ring-a-Bell [27] since it is the most similar attack to our method. Ring-a-Bell requires the target unlearned model’s text encoder for optimization; we use the SD v1.4 text encoder to generate its adversarial prompts. We use the default configuration with a population size of 200, 3000 generations, a mutation rate of 0.25, a crossover rate of 0.5, and a prompt length of 16. We additionally evaluate UnlearnDiffAtk (UDA) from Generate-or-Not [29] as a white-box baseline. Unlike BEAP, UDA uses privileged access to the victim model during adversarial prompt optimization and is therefore reported separately from the query-only attack comparison.

Text Encoder For Similarity Calculation

Because our attack is designed specifically for text-to-image generative models, we focus on the CLIP text encoder, which is a standard component in many of these systems. Moreover, we require a text encoder trained in a multimodal (vision–language) setting so that its representation space captures rich, aligned semantics across both modalities; CLIP satisfies this requirement by being trained jointly on image–text pairs. We do not include alternative text encoders such as BERT [49] in our study, as they are generally not used in text-to-image pipelines and produce representations that are not directly compatible with our target architectures. Throughout our experiments, we employ the CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoder [50] to extract text embeddings and to retrieve semantically similar words. Though we used other text encoders to show the ability of our attack using other CLIP models in section D-D.

Hyperparameter Configuration.

For all experiments, we use DeepSeek-V3.1 [45] as the default LLM (ℒ\mathcal{L}), though tests with alternative models such as Qwen2.5-70B showed no significant difference in results. The number of candidate prompts per iteration is fixed at Q=10Q=10, and the total number of iterations is limited to ℐ=10\mathcal{I}=10. At each step, the top S=3S=3 prompts are selected through softmax sampling based on their ImageReward values. Success thresholds for the three reward signals are set to τimg=0.3\tau_{\text{img}}=0.3 for ImageReward, τaes=0.4\tau_{\text{aes}}=0.4 for Aesthetic Score, and τdet=0.45\tau_{\text{det}}=0.45 for NudeNet. For NudeNet, if the detector flags any of the following labels in the image—EXPOSED ANUS, EXPOSED BREAST F, EXPOSED GENITALIA F, or EXPOSED GENITALIA M—we consider the image to contain nudity. For DINOv2, an image is considered to contain the target object when “golf ball” is its top-1 predicted class. The adversarial similarity vocabulary used for paraphrasing includes the top k=20k=20 words most semantically aligned with the forgotten concept.

Evaluation.

We first quantify how effectively the target concept is removed from the original model by applying each unlearning method to the initial prompts. For nudity evaluation, we use OpenNSFW2 [46], which is not used during BEAP optimization, and classify an image as containing nudity when its NSFW score exceeds 0.5. We report the resulting concept-presence rate as ASROpenNSFW2{}_{\text{OpenNSFW2}}. In the exploratory object-unlearning experiment, DINOv2 is used only as an optimization signal, while a pretrained ResNet-50 classifier [47] provides the held-out evaluation: an image is counted as containing the target object when “golf ball” is the classifier’s top-1 predicted class. We report the resulting rate as ASRResNet-50{}_{\text{ResNet-50}}. ASRAll{}_{\text{All}} additionally requires the ImageReward and Aesthetic Score thresholds in Section B to be met (Tables I and IV). All reported results are averaged over three independent runs. We also report the average ImageReward and Aesthetic scores of the unlearned models on both the original I2P prompts and the corresponding attack prompts (Table II). Because these two metrics are also supplied to the LLM as search feedback, they are optimization-objective diagnostics rather than held-out evaluation metrics. Finally, we examine the detectability of adversarial prompts through perplexity and the Gibberish Detector [30] (Table III). We also measure our average number of iteration needed by our attack to achieve its defined success (Tables I and IV).

Figure 6 provides the full initial prompt delivered to the LLM at the beginning of BEAP’s search process. It includes the task specification, the concept-related vocabulary, and the structured JSON format required for generating the first batch of paraphrased prompts. This figure reflects only the initial instruction stage rather than the subsequent refinement iterations.

Appendix D Ablation

D-A Effect of Top-kk Vocabulary Size

We analyze how the size of the adversarial similarity vocabulary affects BEAP by varying the number of concept-related words k∈{10,20,30}k\in\{10,20,30\}. Figure 7 reports the ASR achieved for each unlearning backbone.

When the vocabulary is too small (k=10k{=}10), the LLM is limited to a narrow set of semantically related terms, which restricts paraphrasing diversity and leads to noticeably lower ASR compared to the default setting (e.g., UCE: 86% vs. 99%; ESD: 72% vs. 95%). Increasing the vocabulary to a moderate size (k=20k{=}20) provides enough linguistic variety to explore useful phrasing changes while keeping the search focused on concept-relevant directions.

However, expanding the vocabulary too far (k=30k{=}30) introduces less relevant or noisy terms, which again degrades performance (e.g., MACE: 97% at k=20k{=}20 drops to 84% at k=30k{=}30). This pattern appears across all models.

Overall, k=20k{=}20 offers the best trade-off between diversity and semantic precision, yielding the most consistent and highest ASR across all unlearning backbones.

D-B Effect of Query Count (QQ)

We evaluate how the number of LLM-generated candidate prompts per iteration affects BEAP’s performance by varying Q∈{5,10,15}Q\in\{5,10,15\}. Figure 8 reports the ASR achieved for each unlearning backbone.

When the query budget is too small (Q=5Q{=}5), the search explores only a limited portion of the paraphrase space, leading to reduced ASR on all models (e.g., UCE: 63% vs. 95% at Q=10Q{=}10; Receler: 88% vs. 97%). Increasing QQ to a moderate level (Q=10Q{=}10) provides sufficient linguistic diversity to reliably reach effective phrasing changes, consistently yielding the strongest results.

Further increasing the query count to Q=15Q{=}15 does not provide consistent improvements. While some models maintain similar performance, others experience a noticeable drop due to redundant or semantically diffuse paraphrases (e.g., UCE: 95% falls to 77%). This indicates that excessively large query sets introduce noise rather than useful expansion.

Overall, Q=10Q{=}10 offers the best balance between exploration and efficiency, enabling BEAP to perform a focused yet diverse search while avoiding unnecessary computation and paraphrase redundancy.

D-C Embedding-Guided Vocabulary Usage

To quantify how effectively BEAP incorporates embedding-guided lexical cues, we measure the average number of guidance words used in the final adversarial prompts across different unlearning backbones. As shown in Table V, BEAP consistently inserts an average of one to two embedding-aligned words per prompt. This demonstrates that the LLM actively leverages the provided semantic cues. Even this small but targeted usage is sufficient to meaningfully steer the paraphrasing process, leading to the clear performance gains observed over BEAP (w/o EG) in both ASR and speed. This confirms that embedding guidance plays a direct and effective role in recovering the forgotten concept.

D-D Effect of Different Text Encoders

To understand how the choice of text encoder affects BEAP, we compare three variants of our method: BEAP (w/o EG), which uses no embedding-guided refinement; BEAP–SD 2.1, which uses the OpenCLIP ViT-H/14 encoder [51]; and BEAP–SD 1.4, which uses the CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder [50]. Both encoders belong to the family of vision–language models, which capture semantic structure grounded in visual data and are therefore suitable for guiding a text-to-image adversarial attack. Non-visual text embeddings (e.g., BERT) were avoided, as they do not reflect the visual semantics required for similarity-based prompting.

As shown in Table VI, BEAP remains effective across all encoders. While performance varies slightly depending on the backbone, the overall trend is stable: both CLIP ViT-L/14 and OpenCLIP ViT-H/14 provide strong, consistent ASR, confirming that BEAP does not depend on a specific encoder. This robustness indicates that any high-quality vision–language encoder can support the embedding-guided prompting component of our framework.

Appendix E Additional Qualitative Results

For completeness, we include extended qualitative examples for both concept-level (nudity) and object-level (golf ball) unlearning. Figures 9 and 10 present additional nudity-related generations across all backbones using the original I2P prompt, Ring-a-Bell, and our method BEAP. Figure 11 shows corresponding qualitative results for the “golf ball” object unlearning task.

Across all settings, BEAP consistently produces natural, meaningful prompts that yield visually coherent and semantically aligned images. In contrast, Ring-a-Bell generates incoherent prompts and distorted outputs, failing to meaningfully recover the concept or object. These extended qualitative samples further demonstrate that unlearned models retain recoverable representations of both concepts and objects, and that BEAP can reliably expose this residual knowledge while maintaining high image quality.
